sections.label: Pallavi
sections.ta:
தூண்டா விளக்கே மாலும் அயனும்
தீண்டா சுடரே அடியார் அகமுறை சிவமே
sections.translit:
thUNdA viLakkE mAlum ayanum
thINdA sudarE adiyAr agamuRai sivamE
sections.en: Lord Siva, you are self-luminous. Thou art the flame, untouched by even the great Vishnu and Brahma. You dwell in the hearts of your devotees.

sections.label: Anupallavi
sections.ta:
அருள் நோக்கினால் மருள் நீக்கியார் தம்
சூலை நோய் போக்கி கறையிலா வாழ்வீந்த
sections.translit:
aruL nOkkinAl maruL nIkkiyAr tham
sUlai nOy pOkki kaRaiyilA vAzhvIndha
sections.en: You cured the severe gastric pain of Marulnikkiyar with a compassionate glance and blessed him with an immaculate life.

sections.label: Charanam
sections.ta:
அறியாப் பருவமென சமணர் குழுவில் அலைந்தவர்
நீற்றறையிலும் வீசிடும் தென்றல் கண்டு
ஆலமும் அமுதென உண்டு கொல் களிறு பணிய
கல்லும் படகாகி மிதந்து கரை சேர்ந்த கதையின் நாயகனே
sections.translit:
aRiyAp paruvamena samaNar kuzhuvil alaindhavar
nItRaRaiyilum vIsidum thendRal kaNdu
Alamum amudhena uNdu kol kaLiRu paNiya
kallum padagAgi midhandhu karai sErndha kadhaiyin nAyaganE
sections.en: Thirunavukkarasar, also known as Appar, strayed in his youth and joined Jainism. He later suffered a severe stomach illness that Jain monks could not cure. According to Saivite tradition, he was healed when his devout sister applied sacred ash and prayed to Shiva. Accused by the Jains of falsely promoting Saivism through this alleged miracle, he faced a series of punishments ordered by the Pallava king. Hagiographies recount that he survived being cast into a lime kiln, given poison, attacked by a royal elephant, and thrown into the sea bound to a stone—all through Shiva’s grace, with the stone said to have floated him safely to shore.

notes: This song is based on the life story of Marulnikkiyar, also known as Thirunavukkarasar/Appar from Sekkizhar’s Peria Puranam. For details, see: பெரிய புராணம், 64-வது நாயனார் தெய்வத்திரு திருமுருக கிருபானந்த வாரியார் சுவாமிகள் வெளியீடு: குகஶ்ரீ வாரியார் பதிப்பகம், 107 சிங்கண்ண தெரு, சிந்தாதிரிப்பேட்டை, சென்னை 600002, தொலைபேசி: 8535666, முதற் பதிப்பு, செப்டம்பர் 2000: பக்கம்: 294 – 308. The Pallavi phrase தூண்டா விளக்கே is a favorite endearment of the Saivites to address Lord Siva. For example, Kripananda Warriar while describing Thilakavathi’s (Thirunavukkarasar’s sister) grief regarding his brother’s departure from Saiva Sidhanta, would pray to Lord Siva. Warriar would state that she prayed to தூண்டா விளக்கனைய சிவசோதி (see the above reference on page 298, paragraph 3). This aligns well with the rest of the Pallavi that refers to Siva appearing as an unkindled fire in Thiruvannamalai. Siva manifested as a towering column of fire, requiring neither wick nor flame, radiating as the brilliant embodiment of eternal knowledge. Through this divine display, he sought to reveal his supremacy to Brahma and Vishnu. In awe, Brahma ascended upward and Vishnu descended downward along the endless pillar, each searching for its crown and feet—but neither could find its beginning nor its end. For details, see the link below: Annamalaiyar Temple Sthalapuranam The first line of the charanam requires some context. Everyone in Thirunavukkarasar’s family was a staunch Saivite. His sister was deeply distressed when he joined the Jain monks and began following Jain practices and rituals. Historically, Jains and Saivites engaged in intense religious debates, and at times these conflicts became severe. In certain periods, those who lost royal favor or theological disputes were subjected to punishment. However, Thirunavukkarasar himself did not actively participate in such debates. After he suffered from a severe gastric ailment, his sister applied sacred ash (vibhuti) to his stomach, and he experienced a miraculous recovery. Following this experience, he returned to Saivism and began promoting it. There was no theatrical display or fraudulent claim involved in his recovery. At that time, the Pallava king was said to be a follower of Jainism. Influenced by reports and complaints from Jain monks, the king ordered severe punishments against Thirunavukkarasar, including attempts to execute him in four different ways, as described in the charanam.
